article.title: Why Regression Discontinuity Can Turn a Business Threshold Into a Natural Experiment
article.why: 理解如何利用明確門檻進行局部因果推論。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

sources.label: World Bank DIME Wiki — Regression Discontinuity

paragraphs.en:
Many businesses use thresholds. A customer receives a benefit after spending $1,000. A loan receives extra review above a risk score. A school program accepts applicants whose test score exceeds a cutoff. These rules can sometimes create a valuable opportunity for causal inference through a method called regression discontinuity design, or RDD.

The intuition is simple. Consider customers with annual spend of $999 and $1,001 when $1,000 determines eligibility for a reward. These customers are extremely similar in observed spending, yet one narrowly misses the reward and the other narrowly receives it. If people cannot precisely manipulate which side of the cutoff they land on, observations very close to the threshold may be comparable except for treatment eligibility.

Researchers estimate whether an outcome jumps at the cutoff. For example, the outcome might be next-month spending. We model the relationship between prior spending and next-month spending on both sides of the threshold and ask whether there is a discontinuity exactly where eligibility changes. A visible and statistically credible jump can be evidence of a local causal effect.

The word local is essential. RDD identifies an effect for units near the cutoff, not automatically for everyone. Customers spending $200 may respond differently from customers spending around $1,000. Therefore, a strong RDD result should not be presented as a universal treatment effect without additional assumptions or evidence.

The design also depends on continuity. In the absence of treatment, potential outcomes should change smoothly around the threshold. If another policy changes at exactly $1,000, we cannot easily separate the two effects. Likewise, if sales staff give special attention to customers just above the threshold, the estimated jump may reflect a bundle of changes rather than the reward alone.

Manipulation is another major concern. Suppose customers know the rule and can deliberately move purchases across dates to exceed $1,000. Then people just above and below the cutoff may no longer be naturally comparable. Analysts often inspect the density of the running variable near the cutoff and investigate operational processes that could create suspicious sorting.

Bandwidth choice matters as well. A very wide window provides more observations but compares less similar units and makes the model more dependent on functional-form assumptions. A narrow window improves local comparability but may produce noisy estimates. Robust analyses report results across reasonable bandwidths rather than selecting only the specification with the most attractive result.

In business settings, RDD is especially appealing when randomized experiments are impossible or when a historical policy already created a sharp rule. Loyalty ranks, credit rules, subsidy eligibility, service levels, and operational escalation thresholds can all produce candidate designs. But the presence of a cutoff does not automatically make an RDD valid.

Before using the method, write down the assignment rule precisely. Identify the running variable, cutoff, treatment, and outcome. Ask whether treatment probability truly changes at that point. Then check whether other variables and policies also jump there, whether the running variable can be manipulated, and whether enough observations exist close to the threshold.

The final communication should emphasize what the design can and cannot claim. Instead of saying “the reward increases spending for all customers,” a careful statement might say, “Among customers near the $1,000 eligibility threshold, crossing the cutoff is associated with an estimated increase consistent with a local causal effect, subject to the continuity and no-manipulation assumptions.” That wording is less dramatic, but it is much more useful for responsible decisions.
